title: Local Success Does Not Compose
one_liner: LLMs write correct specs for one function but fail catastrophically when functions must talk to each other through shared data.
lead: LLMs are very good at writing specifications (the mathematical guarantees) for single functions in isolation: syntax error rates near zero, verification rates above 50%. But the real world does not work in isolation. When a program chains multiple functions together—where the output of one feeds into the input of the next—today's LLMs fall apart. DafnyCOMP is a benchmark that exposes this gap by asking LLMs to write specifications for multi-function programs, and it finds a stunning collapse: verification rates plummet from 58% to 3.69%. This paper argues that current LLMs lack the architectural capacity to reason about how constraints propagate across function boundaries.

paras: Imagine you write a Python function that takes a list of numbers and returns the sum. You want a computer to prove that your code is correct. To do that, you write a specification: a formal contract saying 'if you give me a list of positive integers, I promise to return a value greater than zero.' An LLM can write such a specification very accurately. But here is the catch: real software does not consist of one isolated function. It is a chain. Function A calls Function B, which calls Function C. The output of A becomes the input to B; the output of B becomes the input to C. Each step must preserve the promises made by the previous step. Beginners might try training an LLM on more single-function examples, or asking it to write specifications one at a time without thinking about how they fit together. This breaks because the specifications for A, B, and C interact through shared data flowing from one to the next. If A promises that its output will be positive, but B's specification does not account for that promise, the entire chain shatters.

Current benchmarks mask this weakness. They measure how well LLMs handle one function in isolation—and the results look great: over 99% of generated code is syntactically correct, and over 50% of specifications pass formal verification. But these benchmarks are not testing the hard part: multi-function reasoning.

callout.html: Build a benchmark (DafnyCOMP) with 300 programs, each made by chaining 2 to 5 real functions together with their actual data dependencies, then ask LLMs to write the formal specifications. When you run it, the specs collapse.

steps.text: Take 2–5 independent functions from LeetCode, combine them in a chain by matching data types.
Convert the Python chain to Dafny (a formal-verification language), strip the specifications.
Run the program through Dafny's verifier, strengthen specs iteratively until it passes.
Give the bare Dafny code to an LLM and ask it to regenerate the specifications.
Count how many specs pass formal verification. Compare single-function baselines to compositional chains.

object.h2: The thing that breaks: cross-function reasoning
paras: The paper changes one thing: the scope of the specification task. Instead of asking the LLM to write a spec for one function, it asks the LLM to write specs for multiple functions that must coordinate through shared data.
object.object: the scope: from one function to multiple functions

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: compositional reasoning capacity
hidden.name: Compositional reasoning across function boundaries
paras: The paper does not reduce reasoning to a single number, but it measures three failure modes that reveal a deeper incapacity. Specification fragility: the spec for function A might be too weak (does not promise enough) or too strong (promises more than the code can deliver), leading to downstream functions receiving mismatched inputs. Implementation-proof misalignment: the LLM writes code that works, but the specification does not describe the actual code behavior—they are talking past each other. Reasoning instability: when chaining functions, the LLM loses track of invariants (the facts that must remain true after each step), leading to broken proofs.

The paper estimates this by measuring what fraction of chains verify and then drilling into where the breaks occur. It finds that 39.2% of failures are fragility, 21.7% are misalignment, and 14.1% are instability. These three categories together explain why compositional tasks fail so dramatically—the LLM lacks an internal model of how data constraints flow through a chain.

heat.caption: Darker means more impact on whether the chain verifies. Highlights show where specs are strong but fail to bridge functions.

reads.html: How well does the LLM keep track of promises flowing from one function to the next?
Specification fragility (39.2%), implementation-proof misalignment (21.7%), reasoning instability (14.1%).

mechanism.h2: Why LLMs fail at compositional specs
paras: Here is the core: attention mechanisms (the core of how transformers work—the way the model attends to relevant parts of the input) are designed to capture local dependencies: 'If I see a variable x on line 5, find where x was defined on line 3 and use both together.' But specifications for chained functions require bidirectional reasoning: 'Function A promises to output positive integers; does B's spec account for that? Does B's postcondition (what it promises to output) satisfy C's input requirements?' The transformer must track abstract guarantees across function boundaries, not just concrete tokens on a page. Transformers excel at pattern matching ('I have seen specs like this before') but not at principled proof construction ('Does this spec actually logically entail the next step?'). When functions are combined in ways the model's training data did not show, pattern matching fails. A spec that 'looks right' based on training patterns does not guarantee that it aligns with downstream code.

The paper shows that even the largest models (480 billion parameters) fail as badly as much smaller models (32 billion) at compositional tasks. This suggests it is not a matter of scale—the architectural primitives are missing. Transformers were not built to reason about compositional constraints; they were built to predict the next word given the previous ones. When you ask an LLM to reason about new combinations of functions it has never seen before (rather than matching existing patterns), it breaks down. The machinery to propagate a logical requirement backwards through a chain of functions simply is not there.

stages.s: Program: FuncA chained to FuncB chained to FuncC
LLM reads code and specs for A
LLM generates spec for A using local patterns
LLM reads code and specs for B, sees that B expects X as input
LLM must confirm A's output matches B's input—bidirectional reasoning required here, breaks down
LLM generates spec for B anyway, misaligned
Verification fails: A's promise does not match B's expectation

math.words: For each function, a Dafny spec has a precondition (input requirement), a postcondition (output promise), and loop invariants (facts that stay true during iteration). For a chain A then B, A's postcondition must imply B's precondition. If not, verification fails.
math.equation: verify(chain) = A.postcondition => B.precondition AND B.postcondition => C.precondition
symbols: what function A promises to output
what function B requires as input
whether the entire chain satisfies the proof checker

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Function A: given a list of integers, return the sum. Postcondition: result >= 0 (if all inputs >= 0).
Function B: given a number, return its square root. Precondition: input > 0.
LLM writes A's spec correctly: result >= 0. But B requires input > 0. Equality failed: >= is weaker than >.
Verifier rejects the chain because B might receive 0 from A (e.g., empty list sum), violating the requirement.

math.note: The math captures the core: compositional verification is about logical implication along a chain, not isolated correctness.

charts.title: Single function (prior benchmarks)
charts.note: Earlier benchmarks measured one function at a time. Results look strong.

charts.title: Compositional (DafnyCOMP)
charts.note: When functions must coordinate, everything collapses. 92% performance gap.

items.html: The spec for one function is too weak or too strong. Weak: it does not promise enough, so the next function in the chain receives garbage. Strong: it promises more than the code delivers, making the proof impossible.

The code works correctly, but the spec does not describe it accurately. The LLM treats them as independent tasks: 'Write code that works' and separately 'Write a spec that looks right.' They do not talk to each other.
Over a chain of multiple functions, the LLM loses invariants: the facts that must stay true. A loop invariant is forgotten. A precondition needed three steps earlier is omitted.

Humans can write compositional specs because they reason logically about constraints. They know that if function A outputs a list, function B must handle a list. This is not pattern matching; it is reasoning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a mini suite: take any three simple functions (e.g., list-sum, integer-square-root, minimum-finder). Chain them: sum a list, take the square root of the sum, find the minimum across multiple summed lists. Ask an LLM to write Dafny specs for the chain. Run the Dafny verifier. Count how many of the three specs pass together. Then remove the chaining constraint: ask the LLM to spec each function in isolation. Verify each one separately. The contrast should be stark: high pass rate individually, zero pass rate jointly.
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss this truth: LLMs know how to write specs, but they do not know how to write specs that coordinate across function boundaries. It is not a skill gap. It is an architectural gap.
